prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of who exports and invests abroad and how trade generates gains through reallocation across firms.

statement.case_for: I keep B001 first after reading the openings. The discovery is a single, well-defined idea: productivity differences across firms drive selection into exporting and foreign direct investment, so trade reallocates activity within industries. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) gave a tractable model with sharp, testable predictions, and the predictions were tested in firm-level microdata across many countries. It also changed practice outside trade. Macro, development and productivity researchers, and policy modellers who evaluate liberalisation, now use heterogeneous-firm models as a workhorse. The core papers are more than twenty years old, so the record has had time to be tested, and where the baseline predictions fail in detail the model has been extended rather than abandoned. Attribution to the two named laureates is the cleanest available on the ballot. Melitz supplied the central selection model, and Helpman combined the monopolistic-competition foundations with the exports-versus-FDI margin. I read this as a conceptual reorientation of a field rather than a toolkit, and I weigh that heavily. I have not independently verified the priority record, and I am not treating the number of colleagues who ranked it first as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related and in part parallel contributions, and they are outside the credited set. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is also excluded. A two-name prize could therefore look like it under-credits the empirical firm-level facts and the quantitative-trade lineage. Part of the new-trade-theory lineage was recognised with Krugman in 2008. The baseline Melitz model's welfare implications also depend on distributional and functional-form assumptions, so the size of the extra gains from trade is still debated. If the Committee judged the achievement to be the whole firm-level trade agenda rather than the selection model, this ballot entry would be too narrow.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first. He sees the BLP demand framework and the dynamic-oligopoly methods as cleanly attributable to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, as fully mature, and as widely used in merger review, antitrust, trade and environmental policy. He ranks B001 second and notes overlap with B037 and B047 through Helpman.
responses.response: I agree that BLP attribution is unusually clean and the applied reach is large. I ranked B006 second for that reason, and I treat it as the strongest alternative. Where I differ is on kind of contribution. BLP changed how researchers estimate, while heterogeneous-firm trade changed what the field takes the object of analysis to be, and it created new theoretical channels for gains from trade. I also see a boundary problem in B006 that is absent in B001: whether the discovery is demand estimation or dynamic games, and whether Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are in or out. On the Helpman overlap, I would keep the citation to the firm-selection and FDI-sorting achievement. His political-economy-of-protection work with Grossman (B047) is a different achievement, and the overlap does not weaken the case here.

responses.point: Krusell treats Melitz as central and Helpman as the natural co-recipient. He sees Redding as a major but more derivative third name, so two laureates give the cleanest attribution. He also notes that the Melitz model is used in macro and policy analysis.
responses.response: I agree with the two-name attribution, and I would add one qualification. Redding's contribution is better judged as a separate achievement, the quantitative and spatial trade lineage in B037, than as a derivative of this one. Adding him would blur the citation. I also agree that the framework's use beyond trade supports the case. Your disclosure about field proximity is a reminder that my own closeness to pricing and trade could bias me. For that reason I rest the case on the documented firm-level evidence and not on my sense of the field.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B006 first. He stresses its impact beyond industrial organisation and notes that IO has not been recognised since 2014 and trade not since 2008. He ranks B001 second and flags credit overlap with Bernard, Eaton and Kortum.
responses.response: I share the attribution concern, and it is the main reason I list it as my central uncertainty. I would not count field rotation as scientific merit, though. Both fields have gone unrecognised for long, so the argument does not separate B001 from B006. Both candidates have decades of confirmation. The distinction I would stress is conceptual influence beyond the home field, and on that I think B001 is slightly stronger. If the Committee finds the Bernard-Eaton-Kortum-Jensen parallel work too entangled for a clean citation, that is the point at which I would move toward B006.

responses.point: Teorell supports Helpman and Melitz, with Melitz as the core and Helpman as the complement. He cautions that some predictions of the baseline model are rejected in detail and that the Committee may weigh Helpman's earlier new-trade-theory work differently.
responses.response: I agree that some baseline predictions fail in detail. I count that as a sign of a productive framework rather than a weakness, because the failures led to extensions that kept the selection logic. It still bears on how the citation is worded. I would credit the introduction of firm heterogeneity and selection, not a specific welfare magnitude, since the quantitative size of the gains depends on modelling assumptions. On Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work, I think it strengthens his claim here as a foundation, and I do not want the citation to depend on the 2008 prize's scope.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would treat Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as co-originators in a way that makes a two-name award on this ballot entry hard to defend.

Whether the right framing is the heterogeneous-firm selection model (B001) or a broader trade prize combined with the quantitative-trade lineage (B037) or with B047. I cannot resolve this from the supplied evidence.
How far the sensitivity of the welfare-gain magnitudes to distributional assumptions should limit the wording of the citation.
How to weigh a conceptual reorientation (B001) against a widely used methodological toolkit with clean attribution (B006), since I rank B006 second.
I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or award history.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any credited name on the shortlist is apparent from my profile. For transparency: I co-authored a menu-cost paper (IJIO 2026, not on the shortlist) with the chair John Hassler and with Tore Ellingsen. My research in exchange-rate pass-through, invoicing currency and imperfect-competition pricing is adjacent to trade and industrial organisation, which may bias my view of B001 and B006. My spouse is Magdalena Andersson, a public fact noted only for disclosure, and no bearing on any shortlisted candidate is apparent.
